Type Green infrastructure Related term Rain garden, bioretention [1] Valley example Elmer Avenue, Sun Valley [2] Reported capacity 24 swales treat 115,000 gal [2] Related Permeable paving Figures link to Notes below. Contents What it is Case: Elmer Avenue Applying it to a parking lot See also Notes What it is # A bioswale is a shallow planted channel or bed that takes in runoff from a road, roof or lot and lets it soak into the ground. It is a close relative of the rain garden. The EPA describes a rain garden as a depressed area in the landscape that collects rain from a roof, driveway or street and lets it soak in, planted with grasses and flowering perennials. It can also filter pollutants and shelter wildlife. More complex versions with drainage systems and amended soils are often called bioretention. [1] Case: Elmer Avenue # Elmer Avenue in Sun Valley was a street with no pedestrian or stormwater infrastructure and frequent flooding. The retrofit captures and filters runoff from a 40-acre area. [2] The project reports: 24 bioswales that together can capture and treat 115,000 gallons of runoff and add 1,728 square feet of planting. Up to 5.4 million gallons of stormwater infiltrated per year, and reduced lead, copper and suspended solids concentrations by 60%, 33% and 18%. 23 native trees along the sidewalks. Residents satisfied with the block’s walkability rising from under 2% of survey respondents in 2006 to 92% in 2011. Those are figures reported by the project’s case study brief, not independent audits. The survey is also small and self-reported. [2] Applying it to a parking lot # In my Topanga Willows study I turn the strip where car noses overhang at the edge of a lot into a swale, with curb cuts that let runoff in. [3] That is a concept, drawn from a street-scale precedent: Elmer Avenue is a residential street, not a retail lot, and I do not know how the soil under any Woodland Hills lot drains. A percolation test would come before any design is real. Type Paving strategy Mechanisms Reflect more sun, evaporate water, or both [1] Arizona pilot Asphalt up to 152°F; cool pavement 10–16°F cooler [1] LA program 175+ lane miles [2] Main caution Can feel hotter to pedestrians [2] Figures link to Notes below. Contents What it is Los Angeles’s experience My working rule What I do not know See also Notes What it is # The EPA uses cool pavement for paving materials that reflect more solar energy, enhance water evaporation, or have otherwise been modified to stay cooler than conventional pavements. It can be made with ordinary asphalt and concrete, with coatings, or with grass paving. [1] A pilot study in Arizona found conventional paving such as asphalt reaching surface temperatures up to 152°F at midday, while cool pavements stayed 10 to 16°F cooler. [1] Los Angeles’s experience # Los Angeles has spent millions installing “cool” pavement on more than 175 lane miles across the city. [2] But a UCLA study discussed by NBC Los Angeles says more research is needed to know the real benefits: cool pavement may lower surface temperatures yet feel hotter to a person, in part because the effect of sunlight is increased as heat re-radiates from the pavement. [2] I read that as a lesson in what to measure. Surface temperature is easy to read with a thermometer; comfort depends on air temperature, wind, humidity and radiation from every surface around a person. My working rule # This is my design judgment, not a sourced finding: shade first, and use reflective coatings only where people are not standing, such as drive aisles. My Topanga Willows study follows that order. [3] What I do not know # Limits of this entry I read the UCLA findings through a news report, not the report itself, so I state them at the level of detail the report gave. The Arizona figures are from one pilot, not a Los Angeles measurement. pages.x: Impervious surface | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Impervious surface Any hard cover that rain cannot soak through Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Impervious surface Rain on hard cover runs off. Concept sketch. Type Land-cover category Examples Roofs, roads, driveways, parking lots Effect More runoff, less infiltration [1] Linked risk More frequent, more severe floods [1] Fixes Bioswales , permeable paving Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What happens to the water The heat link In the Valley What I do not know See also Notes What it is # An impervious surface is one that rain cannot pass through. The USGS gives the everyday examples: superhighways, streets, pavement, driveways and house roofs. [1] Land that is natural or planted can take in rain; hard cover sends it somewhere else. What happens to the water # In a forested watershed a significant share of rainfall is absorbed into the soil, stored as groundwater and released slowly to streams. When a watershed urbanizes and vegetation is replaced by impervious cover, there is less area where rain can infiltrate, so more runoff has to be collected by curbs, storm sewers and ditches and carried straight to streams. In a developed watershed much more water reaches a stream much more quickly, and the USGS states that severe flood events happen more often as impervious area grows. [1] The heat link # Impervious cover is also hard and dry, which is why it appears in the EPA’s list of heat island causes: hard, dry surfaces provide less shade and moisture than natural landscapes. [2] A parking lot is both problems at once, which is why I treat permeable paving and bioswales as part of the cooling design and not only the drainage design. In the Valley # Two Valley projects show the other direction. On Elmer Avenue in Sun Valley, a street with no pedestrian or stormwater infrastructure and frequent flooding was retrofitted so that bioswales and a buried infiltration gallery capture runoff from a 40-acre area. [3] The Tujunga Wash, a 13-mile tributary of the Los Angeles River, was channelized for flood control in the 1950s; [4] see riparian corridor for the greenway built beside it. What I do not know # Limits of this entry I do not have a percent-impervious figure for the Valley or for any site I have studied. For a site, I estimate it from aerial imagery, and I label it as an estimate. Contents Where it starts The river in the Valley Why it matters to a small place What I do not know See also Notes Where it starts # The Los Angeles River’s official beginning is the confluence of two channelized streams, Bell Creek and Arroyo Calabasas, in the Canoga Park part of Los Angeles, just east of State Route 27, which is Topanga Canyon Boulevard. [1] From there it flows about 51 miles through the San Fernando Valley, downtown Los Angeles and the Gateway Cities to San Pedro Bay at Long Beach, draining a watershed of about 827 square miles. [1] My first study site is on that same boulevard, though I have not traced where its runoff goes. The river in the Valley # The Sepulveda Basin is a flood-control basin and, with the Griffith Park area and the Willow Avenue estuary in Long Beach, one of only three stretches with a soft bottom. [2] The Tujunga Wash is a 13-mile urban tributary that was channelized for flood control in the 1950s. [3] Why it matters to a small place # Most of the river is a concrete channel designed to move floodwater out quickly, which is the same logic as a storm drain on a parking lot (see impervious surface ). The revitalization office reports that only the Sepulveda Basin and the Glendale Narrows presently support riparian habitat in the 32-mile project area. [4] A site that holds water and plants native trees is a small version of what the river lost (see riparian corridor ). What I do not know # Limits of this entry Length and basin size come from Wikipedia, which I use only for basic geography. I have not confirmed the 51-mile and 827-square-mile figures against a primary source, such as the Army Corps of Engineers or the county, so treat them as approximate. Type Paving system Kinds Pervious asphalt, pervious concrete, interlocking pavers, plastic grid pavers [1] Main benefit Less runoff, some filtering [1] Valley example Elmer Avenue, Sun Valley [2] Related Bioswale Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Where I have seen it used Heat is a separate question A design judgment, labeled See also Notes What it is # Permeable paving is a family of surfaces that let rain and snowmelt seep through to underlying layers of soil and gravel. The EPA lists pervious asphalt, pervious concrete, interlocking pavers and plastic grid pavers. Besides cutting runoff, permeable pavements can filter pollutants and, by reducing the need for some conventional drainage features, reduce construction costs for residential and commercial development. [1] Where I have seen it used # The Elmer Avenue retrofit in Sun Valley installed 63 square feet of permeable concrete and 1,560 square feet of permeable pavers, alongside its bioswales. [2] Heat is a separate question # The EPA groups permeable surfaces under “cool pavements” because they can stay cooler by letting water evaporate. [3] But the cooling depends on moisture, and in a dry Valley summer I do not know how much of it is there. I treat permeable paving as a water measure first and a possible heat bonus second. For surface heat, see cool pavement . A design judgment, labeled # In my Topanga Willows study I put pavers under the parked stalls but keep asphalt in the drive aisles. That is my judgment about turning loads, not a rule I found in a source, [4] and it is the kind of detail an engineer would have to confirm. Permeable systems also need upkeep to stay open, and I have no cost or maintenance figures for Los Angeles. pages.x: Riparian corridor | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Water and ground Riparian corridor The strip of living habitat along a stream or river Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 4 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Riparian corridor A bank with and without a planted edge. Concept sketch. Type Habitat and landscape type Where, in LA Sepulveda Basin; Glendale Narrows [1] Loss, LA River 90–95% of in-stream riparian habitat [1] Valley example Tujunga Wash Greenway, 15 acres [2] Related Los Angeles River Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What was lost Sepulveda Basin Tujunga Wash Greenway Why a small site cares See also Notes What it is # A riparian corridor is the band of plants, soil and wildlife habitat beside a stream. Before the Los Angeles River was channelized, the areas next to it were riparian ecosystems with many native plant and animal species. [3] What was lost # The City of Los Angeles’s river revitalization office cites the California Coastal Conservancy: close to 100% of the original wetlands and 90–95% of in-stream riparian habitat in the Los Angeles River watershed have been lost to urbanization and channelization. Within the 32-mile river project area, the only places that currently support riparian habitat are the Sepulveda Basin and the Glendale Narrows, and both are stressed by exotic species, changed hydrology, dumped trash and encroaching development. [1] Sepulveda Basin # The Sepulveda Basin in the Valley is one of three places along the river with a soft bottom, and native willows dominate the banks between Burbank and Balboa Boulevards, though some non-native trees such as eucalyptus tower over the lower native shrubs. [4] The basin is also a flood-control basin, so the habitat and the engineering share the same ground. Tujunga Wash Greenway # A built example: the 1.2-mile Tujunga Wash Greenway turned an inaccessible right-of-way along a concrete flood channel into 15 acres of riparian habitat, 50 to 60 feet wide, planted with 1,100 trees and 18,000 shrubs and vines, all California natives. A naturalized streambed is fed by up to 325,000 gallons a day diverted from the channel. The project reports it infiltrates up to 118 million gallons of water a year from the channel, recharging the San Fernando groundwater basin, and cuts potential landscape water use by 70–80% by using native plants. [2] These are the project team’s reported figures from a case study brief, not independent measurements. Why a small site cares # My studies are not on river banks. But the Valley’s streets and lots drain toward these channels, so what I do with rain on a parking lot is the first link of the same system. See bioswale and impervious surface . Contents The setting Why it runs hot Water and ground Studies here What I do not know See also Notes The setting # The San Fernando Valley, “the Valley” locally, is an urbanized valley in Los Angeles County, north of the Los Angeles Basin. It covers about 260 square miles and had about 1.8 million people in 2023. It is bounded by the Santa Susana Mountains to the northwest, the Simi Hills to the west, the Santa Monica Mountains to the south, the Verdugo Mountains to the east and the San Gabriel Mountains to the northeast. [1] It includes a large part of the City of Los Angeles plus Burbank, Calabasas, Glendale, Hidden Hills, San Fernando and several unincorporated areas. [1] Why it runs hot # Because of its relatively inland position and other factors, summer days in the Valley are typically hotter, and winter nights colder, than in the Los Angeles Basin. [1] The extreme is Woodland Hills: on Sept. 6, 2020 the official site at Pierce College reached 121°F, the highest temperature ever recorded at an official station in Los Angeles County; it was reached at about 1:30 p.m. [2] [3] That is a single day, and a record at one station, but it is the reason I picked this part of the city. The mechanics of why built-up places stay hotter are in urban heat island . Water and ground # The Valley holds the headwaters and a long reach of the Los Angeles River , with tributaries such as the Tujunga Wash, and some of the clearest examples of retrofitting hard ground to take rain, such as the Elmer Avenue project in Sun Valley. [4] Studies here # My first study is a shopping center in Woodland Hills: Topanga Willows . [5] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The area, population and mountain boundaries come from Wikipedia, which I use for basic geography only. The Valley is not one climate: temperatures vary by neighborhood and elevation, and I have not compared stations. pages.x: Shade equity | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Shade equity Equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~2 min Sources 5 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Shade equity Same street length, two kinds of walk. Concept sketch. Type Planning concept Definition Equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover [1] Facets Distributional, recognitional, procedural Tools Tree Equity Score, canopy maps Related Tree canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is What the evidence shows Three kinds of fairness What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Shade equity is equal access to the cooling benefits of tree cover. [1] The idea is that shade is not a luxury: on a hot day it is the difference between a walk to the bus that is tolerable and one that is not, and it is spread unevenly. What the evidence shows # In Los Angeles, TreePeople’s canopy report found that much of the city’s canopy is “not where the people are,” and that some residents live virtually in a forest while many others live in virtually treeless environments. [2] The national picture is similar. The National Equity Atlas reports that across racial and ethnic groups in urban areas, people living below the federal poverty level have lower tree canopy coverage than those above it. [3] American Forests built the Tree Equity Score to prioritize investment where need is greatest. [4] A 2025 study modeled street trees in one low-income and one high-income Los Angeles neighborhood under two sets of spacing guidelines. Structural differences such as parcel size, intersection density and street width limited how many trees each neighborhood could host. Looser guidelines narrowed the gap in tree numbers , but substantial gaps remained in tree stature, a proxy for canopy. The authors conclude that shade equity may be hard to fix by changing guidelines alone. [5] Three kinds of fairness # The Union of Concerned Scientists argues that growing shade should account for more than where trees physically stand. Distributional equity is the map of who has trees. Recognitional equity means understanding the conditions and root causes, and engaging residents about their own goals and concerns. Procedural equity means transparent decisions and fair access to them. [1] I take that last point seriously for my own work. My studies are drawn from aerial imagery and public research, and they are concept studies. They are not a substitute for asking the people who use a place what they need from it. What I do not know # Limits of this entry The UCS piece is an advocacy-science blog post, and I read the Tree Equity Score and National Equity Atlas pages only as summaries. I have not checked the Valley’s shade distribution myself. The Messier study covers two neighborhoods, so I treat it as a case, not a rule. pages.x: Soil volume | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Soil volume How much root-friendly ground a tree gets, and why that decides whether lot trees live Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~1 min Sources 2 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Soil volume A tree is half underground. Concept sketch. Type Planting design measure Guideline 2–3 cu ft of soil per 1 sq ft of crown spread [1] Field result Every tree with ≥1,500 cu ft was in good condition [2] Sample 1,127 trees, Walt Disney World [2] Related Tree canopy Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is A published guideline A field test What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Soil volume is the amount of uncompacted soil a tree’s roots can reach. In a parking lot it is the problem: a tree in a small paved island is, in the words of a Virginia Tech fact sheet, in a kind of pseudo-container. [1] A published guideline # The Virginia Tech fact sheet advises designing lot islands with as much soil volume as possible, ideally letting roots grow at least to the drip line, the edge of the crown, at maturity. It recommends 2 to 3 cubic feet of soil per 1 square foot of crown spread. [1] Worked example (my arithmetic) Take a tree whose mature crown is 30 feet across. The crown covers about π × 15² ≈ 707 square feet. At 2–3 cubic feet per square foot, that is about 1,400 to 2,100 cubic feet of soil, or a bed 3 feet deep and about 470 to 700 square feet. That is more than many parking islands provide, which is why soil, not the tree, is the hard part. A field test # A study of 1,127 parking lot trees at Walt Disney World found 81% in good condition and only 3% dead since planting, and that every tree in at least 1,500 cubic feet of soil was in good condition. Live oaks ( Quercus virginiana ) planted in groups did better than those planted singly. The authors also say existing planting recommendations were only imperfectly applicable to the site. [2] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The Disney lots are in Florida with different soil, species and irrigation than a Woodland Hills lot, and the 1,500 cubic feet result is for that sample. I do not know the soil under any Valley lot I have studied. A site would need a soil test and an arborist before I put numbers on a tree. pages.d: What “percent canopy” measures, Los Angeles’s numbers, and why canopy is not the same as shade on a sidewalk.
h: Canopy is not the same as shade#
pages.x: Tree canopy | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Trees and shade Tree canopy The share of ground covered by tree leaves and branches, seen from above Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~2 min Sources 2 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Tree canopy Canopy is the view from above. Concept sketch. Type Land-cover measure Unit Percent of land under tree crowns LA County About 18% [1] City of LA About 25% [1] Data year Circa 2016 Related Shade equity , soil volume Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is It is not spread evenly Canopy is not the same as shade What I do not know See also Notes What it is # Tree canopy is the layer of leaves, branches and stems that cover the ground when you look straight down. “Percent canopy” is the share of an area under that layer. It is the standard way cities count their urban forest because it can be estimated from aerial imagery instead of counted tree by tree. An analysis of land cover data from about 2016 found that 18% of Los Angeles County and 25% of the City of Los Angeles was covered by tree canopy. [1] That 25% is the number I cite for the city in my studies. It is not spread evenly # The same report found that five census block groups, one in Pacific Palisades, one in Los Feliz, two in Brentwood and one in Shadow Hills, hold 18% of the city’s total tree canopy while less than 1% of the city’s population lives there. [1] The authors point to a cause: more affluent residents can afford the hill areas, which are better suited to trees and less densely developed. [1] The Union of Concerned Scientists repeats the same pattern, nearly 20% of the urban forest where 1% of people live. [2] That unevenness is the subject of shade equity . Canopy is not the same as shade # This is my own reasoning, not a sourced finding: a percent canopy figure averages over an area, but a person stands at one spot. A neighborhood can have healthy canopy in back yards and none over its bus stops. And a young tree counts as a dot from above while casting almost no shade for years. When I plan planting on a site I therefore ask where the shade lands, at what hour, over what people are doing, and how big the tree will be when it is mature. Getting a tree to maturity in a paved lot depends mostly on what is underground, which is the subject of soil volume . What I do not know # Limits of this entry The 18% and 25% figures come from one 2016-era land cover analysis and will have changed. I do not have a canopy number for the Valley as a whole, for Woodland Hills, or for any block I have studied. I would need the county’s canopy layer clipped to a site to state one. pages.d: Why built-up places run hotter than their surroundings, and the five causes that matter on a parking lot.
pages.x: Urban heat island | Field guide | Redrawn Valley Field guide · Heat Urban heat island Why built-up places run hotter than the land around them Reviewed Nov. 20, 2026 Read ~3 min Sources 3 Part of the Redrawn Valley field guide . Claims link to numbered notes; what I could not verify is said in the text. For a worked site, see the Topanga Willows study . Urban heat island Same sun, different surfaces. Concept sketch. Type Climate effect Also called UHI, heat island Size, U.S. Day: about 1–7°F warmer. Night: about 2–5°F warmer [1] Two kinds Surface and atmospheric Main levers Shade, vegetation, reflective surfaces, less paving Seen in San Fernando Valley Figures link to Notes below. Estimates are labeled. Contents What it is Five causes Surface and atmospheric Why it matters In the Valley What I do not know See also Notes What it is # An urban heat island is a city or neighborhood that is measurably warmer than the less built-up land around it. The U.S. EPA summarizes the research this way: in the United States, daytime temperatures in urban areas run about 1–7°F higher than in outlying areas, and nighttime temperatures about 2–5°F higher. [1] The gap is usually measured as a difference between a city and its surroundings, so it depends on which surroundings you pick. A heat island is not the same thing as a heat wave. A heat wave is weather. A heat island is a built-in offset that rides on top of the weather, and it is largest on the calm, clear days when the weather is already dangerous. [1] Five causes # The EPA lists five, and each one shows up on an ordinary parking lot: [1] Fewer natural landscapes. Trees, plants and water cool the air by shading, by releasing water from leaves, and by evaporation. Hard, dry surfaces such as roofs, sidewalks, roads and parking lots do less of all three. Material properties. Conventional pavement and roofing reflect less solar energy and absorb and emit more heat than vegetation. Heat islands often build through the day and become stronger after sunset as that stored heat leaks out slowly. Urban geometry. Tall buildings and narrow streets trap heat and block wind. Waste heat. Vehicles, air conditioners, buildings and industry all release heat. Weather and geography. Calm, clear weather makes heat islands worse. Wind and cloud cover suppress them. Nearby mountains can block wind or redirect it. The first two are the ones a small site can change. That is why my studies spend their effort on tree canopy and on what the ground is made of ( impervious surface , cool pavement ). Surface and atmospheric # The term covers two different measurements. A surface heat island is how hot the ground and roofs themselves get, which is what a satellite sees. The EPA notes that on a warm day conventional roofing can reach as much as 66°F warmer than the surrounding air. [1] An atmospheric heat island is the warmer air, which is what a thermometer in the shade reads. The EPA says atmospheric heat islands vary much less in intensity than surface ones. [1] This matters for design claims. A pavement that is 15°F cooler at the surface has not made the air 15°F cooler, and a person standing on it feels more than air temperature (see cool pavement ). Why it matters # The EPA ties heat islands to three costs. Electricity demand for air conditioning rises about 1–9% for each 2°F increase in temperature. Higher demand means more fossil-fuel emissions, and more sun and heat means more ground-level ozone. And hot weather contributes to heat-related illness and death, with older adults, young children, low-income populations, people who work outdoors and people with chronic conditions at greatest risk. From 2004 to 2018 the CDC recorded an average of 702 heat deaths per year in the U.S. [1] In the Valley # The Valley is a plausible heat island host: it is inland, ringed by mountains, and summer days there are typically hotter than in the Los Angeles Basin. [2] Its all-time county record is a weather fact, not a heat-island measurement, but it shows the baseline a built-up block starts from: 121°F at Pierce College in Woodland Hills on Sept. 6, 2020. [3] What I do not know # Limits of this entry The 1–7°F and 2–5°F figures are a national range from a review of studies, not a measurement of the Valley. I have not found a published heat island magnitude for a specific Valley block, and I have not measured one. If I want to claim one for a study site, I need paired temperature readings at the site and at a shaded reference, taken the same hour. pages.x: Thirty-eight icons and a logo, drawn as lists of points | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Icons Thirty-eight icons and a logo, drawn as lists of points A small hand-drawn icon set and a ridgeline logo carry the navigation, the phone tab bar and every index row. This is how they are drawn, why the first version was thrown out, and the rules that keep new icons consistent. By Nathan Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 3 sources Lab 2 of 5 01 What the icons are for The site had text links and nothing else, and on a phone the bottom tab bar needs a symbol for every tab. I wanted a set that looks drawn rather than printed, small enough to ship as one file, and consistent enough that a new icon could be added by someone following the written rules. icons: 7 navigation, 16 interface, 15 topic 38 drawing grid 24 px line weight at 24px 1.9 px strokes in the logo 3 The set covers three jobs. Navigation icons sit in the header, the search button and the phone tab bar. Interface icons are arrows, chevrons, a check, a warning and similar. Topic icons start each row of the Field Guide, notes and studies indexes: heat, tree, shade, pavement, water, river, soil, sidewalk, bioswale, permeable paving, leaf, thermometer, pin, ruler and building. 02 How they are made Each icon is a short list of points on a 24 by 24 grid, written by hand in scripts/build_icons.py . The script then roughens the points with a seeded wobble, so the output is stable from run to run, and writes the sprite, the logo, the favicon and a names file that the gallery reads. I never edit the sprite directly: I edit the point list and run the script. A stroke can be a polyline with sharp corners, a smooth curve through points, a closed shape, or a circle. Any stroke can be marked as the accent, and any can lay a pale tint under it that is printed slightly off the line, like a marker that missed the edge. Linework uses currentColor , the accent uses one token, and the tint uses another, so a single CSS class recolors an icon (moss for trees, slate for water) without a second drawing. The first version was more detailed. I replaced it the same day with a set of two or three strokes per icon, a bolder line and a three-stroke logo, because fine detail does not survive at the sizes used beside body text. That is my judgment from looking at the icons at 16, 24 and 32 pixels. The gallery below is the second version. 03 The mark The logo is two ridgelines forming a valley. The ink line is the valley as it was drawn. The brick line beneath it is the same ridge redrawn, and a small brick sun sits low in the gap. That is the site’s whole idea in three strokes: look at a place, then redraw it. It has to read at 16 pixels because that is the favicon size, so the three-stroke limit is not decoration. In the header it sits left of the wordmark; the favicon is the same mark on a paper tile. Because both are made from the same point lists as the icons, they share the wobble. 04 The decisions I made Two or three strokes per icon, with one accent stroke on the meaningful part The accent is how an icon gets personality without a second color system: the door of the house, the leading edge of the pencil. Anything that needs more strokes is an illustration, not an icon. Cost Some topics (bioswale, permeable paving) are abstract at this size and rely on the label next to them. Never fill with solid ink Solid fills turn into blobs when the line is wobbly and break the sketch feel. Pale tints are allowed because they sit off the line and read as paper and marker. Cost Icons look lighter than a standard UI set next to bold text. Keep the source as point lists, not hand-edited SVG A point list is readable, diffable and easy to restyle; I could make the whole set bolder in one edit, which is what the second version needed. Cost Adding an icon means editing a Python file, which is a barrier for a contributor who only knows SVG. Linework follows the text color Using currentColor means icons work on paper, on the dark footer and in the active tab with no extra assets. Cost A single accent color per icon; no two-accent icons. Ship one sprite, referenced with use One request, cached, and every icon can be restyled in CSS. Cost External sprite references need HTTP, so icons do not appear if you open a page from disk. 05 The live gallery Every icon, at its real size, grouped the way they are used. Click an icon to copy its markup. The sizes and tab-bar sections lower on the page show how they scale. Live demo Open it as its own page → The gallery is generated by scripts/build_icons.py between its gallery markers. 06 What I could not verify Limits of this lab I judged legibility at 16, 24 and 32 pixels by eye on one screen. I did not test the icons with people, or on low-resolution displays. The icons are decorative and hidden from screen readers; the text beside each one carries the meaning. I have not tested that with a screen reader. The count of 38 is read from the generated names file on the day I wrote this and will change as icons are added. pages.x: Ten motifs drawn from reference sheets | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Motifs Ten motifs drawn from reference sheets Before there was a generator, there was a sheet of ten hand-built vector motifs. This is what each one is made from, how its colors are wired, and a sheet you can randomize. By Nathan Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 2 sources Lab 4 of 5 01 Where the pattern system started Before the seeded generator, there was a sheet of ten hand-built SVG motifs. I made it first because I wanted to check that the recipe from the reference library worked as original art before I wrote any code to randomize it. If the static motifs did not look right, a generator would only multiply the problem. motifs on the sheet 10 art-only accent colors proposed 5 flat colors per motif, plus ink and paper 2 to 4 color crossfade 1.2 s 02 What each motif is built from Each one comes from a habit I saw in the references, and each one has a use on the site. Grid-filled solids and split discs. Draw a shape in its flat color, then draw the same shape again filled with a 10 pixel graph-paper pattern at 70% ink. The grid stays on the shape, never the field. Used for hero art, dividers and stat cards. Overlapping circles. Three circles at 85% opacity with multiply blending, centers 70 pixels apart. Used for “evidence overlaps” figures. Set square and protractor. The drafting tool is the illustration: a triangle with a cutout and tick marks, a half disc with ticks every 2 degrees and one brick line as the measured angle. Contours. Nested wobbly rings, every fifth heavier, the same idea as the contour lines in the survey sheets. 2 Halftone. A staggered dot grid whose dot radius falls from one side to the other, for transitions between bands. Plan symbols. Tree canopies with a center dot, a dashed slate flow line, a scale bar, a north arrow and a double border like a drawing sheet. Moss for trees and slate for water, matching the design system. Three-tile collage. Two or three tiles side by side, each one thing, each on its own saturated field. This is the layout of the banners. 1 Pill diagram. Rounded pill labels joined by hairline arrows with pale fills, for process figures such as Site, Measure, Plan. 03 The decisions I made Wire every color as a CSS variable on the figure Each motif exposes --field , --a , --b and so on. Randomizing is then one line of script, and the generator that replaced this sheet could reuse the same idea. Cost The sheet itself uses literal hex values for a few fixed pieces, so it is a lab, not a model of token discipline. Propose five art accents instead of using only the interface colors Brick, moss and slate are too serious for decorative tiles; a field of sky, ochre, rose, kelly or periwinkle reads as the playful flat color the references use. They are for decoration only. Cost Adding colors to the system means updating DESIGN.md, which the pattern work did. Offer drift as a toggle, not a default Drift adds a slow six-pixel slide and the color transition. It is off until you press it, and it never runs under reduced motion. Cost On the sheet, motion is opt-in, which hides it from anyone who does not press the button. Keep the sheet, then build the generator The ten static motifs proved the look first. The generator in the pattern sheet article took them from fixed files to seeded art. Cost The two sheets overlap, and the static one is no longer the source of truth. 04 The live sheet Press Randomize colors to swap each motif’s colors from the palette, Reset to go back, and Drift for the slow motion. Live demo Open it as its own page → Ten vector motifs in Redrawn tokens plus the proposed art accents. 05 What I could not verify Limits of this lab The sheet is a design study. Its colors were chosen by eye against the reference sheets, and I did not run contrast checks because the motifs carry no text of meaning. The motifs are original drawings built from patterns that recur across the references, not traced from any one sheet. I list the sources I looked at so the influence is visible. Now it opens with a drawing, changes pages with a wipe of paper tiles, writes its headings in by hand and answers every click. Here is how that works, what I decided and what it costs. By Nathan Nov. 21, 2026 5 min read 5 sources Lab 5 of 5 01 Why the site moves The site is made of sketches, and a sketch has a before and after: lines appear, then fill in. Pages that just snap from one to the next throw that away. I wanted every moment of waiting (the first load, a reload, a link click) to be a small drawing instead of a blank flash, and I wanted headings to look written rather than printed. The references pushed the same way. The tile collages, grid circles and squares from the reference sheets already work as flat, cut-out shapes, which makes them easy to move: a tile can grow, spin and shrink without any new art. things that play, in kinds 4 opening length, my setting 1.5 s page wipe, cover plus lift about 1.3 s script added to each page, one file 1 02 What plays, and when The opening. On the first visit of a browser session, and on every reload, a sheet of paper tiles covers the page. The logo draws itself, “Redrawn Valley” writes in, a tagline fades up, and the tiles shrink away from the center. Tap the sheet to skip it. The page wipe. Following a link covers the page with tiles that grow outward from where you clicked, with the name of the section you are going to written on them. The next page lifts the same tiles from the same spot, so the two pages feel like one move. Handwritten headings. The page title writes in letter by letter, each letter bouncing on the Wobble font’s bounce axis before it settles, with a pencil squiggle drawn under it. Section headings do the same as they scroll into view. 1 Small answers. A click or tap leaves a quick pencil burst. Links get a wavy underline that sweeps in. Buttons spring and squish. Rows slide and their icons tilt. Rules draw on, and figures get crop marks in their corners for a moment. Back and forward buttons skip the opening and the wipe, because showing an animation on a page you are returning to feels slow. 03 The decisions I made Build the wipe myself instead of using the browser’s page transitions The View Transition API can fade between pages with almost no code, but it is newer, so older browsers get nothing, and it only crossfades snapshots. 2 A script that covers the page, remembers where you clicked, and lifts the cover on the next page works the same everywhere and can show tiles in our own colors. Cost Each navigation waits about 0.8 s before the next page starts to load, a delay the browser’s own transition would not add. Paint a paper sheet before anything else The script sits in the head and adds one CSS rule that paints paper over the page before the first frame, so there is no flash of unstyled content. A five second failsafe removes the sheet if anything goes wrong. Cost It is a blocking script, though a small one, and it hides the page during the opening. Hold the sheet in the top layer The tiles live in a manual popover, which browsers draw above everything including open dialogs, so a link chosen from the search dialog is still covered. 3 Browsers without popovers fall back to a very high z-index. Cost A top-layer sheet cannot be hidden by page code once it is open, so the failsafe has to remove it. Animate tiles with the Web Animations API Over a hundred tiles need staggered delays that depend on their distance from the click. Setting those per tile in code is simpler than generating CSS, and only transforms animate, so the browser can run them on the graphics card. 4 Cost On a very slow phone a hundred animated tiles may drop frames. I have not measured that. Turn everything off for reduced motion Under the reduced-motion setting none of this runs: no opening, no wipe, no dab, and headings stay plain text. Large movement across the whole screen is the kind of motion that setting exists to avoid. 5 Embed frames inside lab articles are off too, so a frame never covers its own article. Cost Those visitors never see the opening drawing. 04 The live demo Replay the opening, try the wipe from three starting points, write a heading again, click the grid for the pencil dab and change the speed. The effects play inside the frame, so they cover only the frame. Live demo Open it as its own page → Every effect on the site, one button each. 05 What I could not verify Limits of this lab All timings (1.5 s, 0.5 s, 0.8 s) are my own settings, tuned by eye on a desktop and a phone-size window. I did not measure frame rate on real phones. I tested in one Chromium build. Safari and Firefox should run it, since it uses long-standing APIs, but I have not seen it there. Each letter of a heading is its own element, and I gave each heading an accessible label with its full text. I have not tried it with a screen reader. pages.x: How every page got its own drawing | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Patterns How every page got its own drawing Every page and note on this site carries a banner drawn from a seed. This is how I got from a folder of reference sheets to fourteen original motifs, what I decided along the way, and a live lab where you can reroll one. By Nathan Nov. 21, 2026 6 min read 4 sources Lab 1 of 5 01 Why generate the art at all The site started as words and a few diagrams. A study or a note with no picture at the top looks unfinished, but I had three rules in the way: no stock imagery, nothing glossy, and no copying another site’s art. Drawing a banner by hand for every page would also not scale, because every new note would need one. So the banners are generated from a seed. The page slug is the seed, which means the same page always gets the same drawing, and a different page gets a different one. That is the whole idea. Everything else in this article is about making the generated drawings look like they came from a sketchbook and not from a random-shape toy. motifs on the pattern sheet 14 colors: 6 interface, 5 art-only 11 layouts: banner, strip, card, square 4 between one tile shifting 5 to 10 s 02 What I studied I kept a reference library in the project files, outside the repo, and built contact sheets from it so I could compare many drawings at once. It has two parts. The first is screenshots of public pages from Anthropic’s site, taken on Nov. 20, 2026, for private study. 1 The second is public-domain drawings from the Historic American Buildings Survey and its sister programs, made for the National Park Service and held by the Library of Congress. I downloaded them from Wikimedia Commons, where each file is marked public domain, and the library’s own notes record that I checked that through the Commons API on Nov. 20. 3 Looking across the sheets, a few habits repeated. The “Building effective agents” hero is a three-tile collage: ink arcs on sage, a drafting compass on green grid paper, a weather-style contour map. 1 Anthropic’s designers describe the intent as soft beige, hand-drawn illustration and “the mark of the maker.” 2 The survey sheets contribute a different vocabulary: contour rings, tree canopies drawn as circles with a center dot, scale bars, north arrows, double-ruled borders. 3 From the contact sheets I wrote down a recipe: two to four flat colors per image plus ink and paper; each tile is one thing; a fine grid sits on a shape and never on the field; drafting tools appear as objects; and ink line weight stays constant inside one drawing. I did not trace anything. The reference pixels stay in the library, and the repo only holds motifs I drew in code. 03 The decisions I made Draw everything in code, from the recipe, not from the pictures The Anthropic art is copyrighted and the survey sheets are public domain but sheet-specific. Drawing each motif in code from the recipe keeps the site original and keeps the files small (one 35 KB script, not a folder of images). It also means every color is a CSS variable, so the art follows the design tokens. Cost More work up front, and no motif is as rich as a real engraved sheet. Seed the randomness with the page slug The same slug always draws the same banner, so a page does not change its look between visits and a bad composition can be fixed by changing one string. Pages without a topic draw from the full set. Cost I cannot hand-tune a single composition; I can only reroll the seed. Two palettes, with a firm rule between them Brick, moss and slate keep their interface jobs: action, link and water. Five extra colors (sky, ochre, rose, kelly and periwinkle), toned from the references, are for decoration only. They never carry text or meaning. Cost The art accents are not contrast-checked as text colors, so the rule is the safeguard. Keep the line weight constant and the grid on the shape This is the most visible habit in the references. It also keeps the generated art from turning into noise when a tile is small. Cost Some compositions look plainer than a freehand drawing would. Move slowly and rarely One tile shifts every five to ten seconds: a color crossfade, a disc turning into a rounded square, a needle swinging. It runs only while the art is at least 10% on screen and the tab is visible, and under reduced motion it stays still. Cost The motion is easy to miss, which is the point, but it means a screenshot never shows it. Bias the art by topic A data-topic leans the palette and motifs toward the subject: shade and trees toward moss and canopy plans, water toward slate and contours, heat toward brick and halftone, soil toward ochre. Cost The mapping is my judgment and is not tested on readers. 04 The live lab This is the same renderer the site uses, with the controls exposed. Type any seed, pick a topic and a layout, press Reroll for a random seed, and watch a tile change its color, shape or icon every few seconds. Pause drift freezes it. pages.x: Choosing a hand for the type | Lab notes | Redrawn Valley ← Lab notes Type Choosing a hand for the type Forty-six font entries screened for license, accents, size and legibility, six type directions built from them, and three ways to write text in. The research, the decision (Wobble, now live site-wide) and the live lab are all here. By Nathan Nov. 21, 2026 7 min read 5 sources Lab 3 of 5 01 The question The site speaks in a serif, sets its interface in a sans, and uses a hand font for eyebrows, tags and notes. I wanted to find out whether a hand-drawn face could carry the site, and which one, without breaking three things I care about: free licenses, Spanish place names with accents, and text that stays readable at caption size on a phone. entries in the research table 46 under the OFL, 7 Apache 2.0 38 directions built and compared 6 ways to write text in 3 The table counts entries, and some entries group two or three related families, so the number of families screened is a little higher. The lab itself says about sixty. 02 What I screened and what I found For each candidate I recorded its license, the size of its Latin-subset file, and which of the glyphs I need are missing. The glyph check reads the font file’s own character map for the accented letters in Spanish place names, the degree sign, dashes, the multiplication sign, fractions and superscripts. Sizes are the woff2 files Google Fonts serves for the Latin subset, read on Nov. 21, 2026. 1 Almost everything is free for websites. 38 entries are under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, which allows self-hosting and embedding with no fee, and seven are Apache 2.0, which also does. 2 The one outlier is the Hershey single-stroke data I use for pen animation, which is free to use with credit. 4 Twenty entries made it into at least one direction and three more earned a place as annotation voices. Twenty-three were rejected, and the reasons cluster. Three have no accented letters at all (Nanum Pen Script, Gaegu and Edu SA Beginner), which breaks on a Spanish place name; Gaegu is also missing the degree sign and the dashes. Several are too thin or faint at caption size (Shadows Into Light, Coming Soon, Sue Ellen Francisco). Several are too wide, so headlines wrap (Gloria Hallelujah, Short Stack). Some read as a child’s card or a friendly app and not as a field sketchbook (Indie Flower, Schoolbell, Mali). The sketch-fill fonts turn to noise below 28 pixels. The complete table, with every font, license and verdict, is inside the lab below. 03 Six directions From the survivors I built six directions, each with a full hierarchy on a sample page so I could judge them in context and not as a specimen line. Field Notebook (Caveat, Kalam, Patrick Hand): looks written on site, and the most personal. Drafting Sheet : architect lettering for the plans. Marker and Brush : bold field-sign lettering. Typewriter Log (Special Elite, Courier Prime): a field log typed up, good where numbers lead. Hand-cut Serif (Fraunces): a serif with a hand in it. Wobble (Shantell Sans): one variable font whose letters can move. Hand fonts are good for titles, labels and notes and poor for long reading. They have small x-heights, uneven rhythm and thin strokes, and none of them read well for more than a few hundred words. That finding shaped every direction: the hand is for the display and the annotation, and the reading text stays a face built for reading. 04 The decisions I made Treat accents as a hard requirement The Valley has Cañada, Topanga and Tujunga on its maps, and a font that drops the ñ is a font that fails on the first page. Missing glyphs are a rejection, not a footnote. Cost It removed three otherwise attractive fonts from the shortlist. Choose Wobble (Shantell Sans) for the whole site My recommendation in the lab was Hand-cut Serif, with Field Notebook for titles, and I ended up choosing Wobble instead. It is one variable font that covers every role, so the site reads as one hand, and its INFM and BNCE axes let titles be looser while body text stays calmer. IBM Plex Mono stays for citations, captions and numbers, so evidence still looks like evidence. The font tokens now all point at Shantell Sans. Cost Hand fonts read slower over long text, which is why the body setting is deliberately calm. At about 170 KB with all axes it is the heaviest option, trimming axes would cut it, and Shantell has no italic file, so italics are synthesized. Add three writing effects with two speeds each A pen write-on from single-stroke Hershey data, a typewriter that strikes keys at irregular times, and a sweep that works on any font. Each has a fast and a slow speed, and under reduced motion nothing plays by itself, though a button you press still plays. Cost The pen effect needs its own letterform data, so accents there are added by code and are approximate. Keep the lab as the record, marked noindex The lab stays on the site as the candidate sheet behind the choice, so the research and the five directions I did not pick remain visible. It is noindex because it is a working page; this article is the readable version. Cost The lab shows six directions but only one is live, so the lab no longer matches the site. 05 The live lab The full lab, embedded. Wobble is Direction 6 and is what the site now uses. Switch the body text between each direction’s own font and the earlier Newsreader, press Replay on any writing effect, and scroll to the bottom for the research table. The frame scrolls on its own; the link opens it full page. Live demo Open it as its own page → Six directions, three writing effects and the full research table. Generated by scripts/build_type_lab.py. 06 What I could not verify Limits of this lab I did not read every license file. I used the license Google Fonts lists for each family and cross-checked it against Fontsource, which agreed for every font here. Glyph coverage was tested on the default weight, not every weight. Playwrite’s download size could not be me

County happened in Woodland Hills A 121-degree reading makes a headline. For a site study, the better question is what the thermometer can and cannot tell me about the block I am drawing. By Nathan Nov. 20, 2026 5 min read 5 sources Note 1 of 5 01 One reading, and what it cannot tell you On September 6, 2020, the official weather station in Woodland Hills recorded 121°F. The National Weather Service said it was the hottest temperature ever recorded at an official station in Los Angeles County. The old record was 119°F, set in July 2006. 1 The same weekend, Burbank appeared to tie its own all-time record at 114°F. 1 The National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office described the Woodland Hills site as the one at Pierce College. 2 I started this site with a Woodland Hills sidewalk, so that number is not trivia to me. But one day is one day. A record is rare by definition, and I do not want to open a study by treating it as typical. What it does tell me is the ceiling: this part of the Valley can do that, and anything I draw for it has to survive that kind of day. Fig. 1 Official air-temperature readings from the L.A. Times report on the September 2020 heat wave, plotted on an axis that starts at 110 °F so the gaps are visible. Burbank’s reading was reported as appearing to tie its all-time record. Notice what the figure does and does not show. It shows three official readings. It does not show how hot any particular street was, because an official station sits in one spot and a sidewalk across town has different surroundings. Treat the number as a ceiling for the region, not a measurement of your block. 02 Heat islands are local, and canopy is what they track Some of the hottest spots in the Valley are not hot because of the Valley. They are hot because of what is on the ground. A study for the California Energy Commission used a calibrated weather model and observations to map neighborhood-scale heat islands across Los Angeles. Its authors include Haider Taha, who also ran the Pacoima cool pavement analysis I come back to in the next note. 3 The sentence in that report that matters most for my work is short. In the San Fernando Valley study area, the largest localized heat islands were associated with the lowest vegetation canopy cover. 3 The report’s model also put higher temperatures in the industrial and commercial areas running from near Chatsworth down through Canoga Park and Woodland Hills, and along major roads such as Sherman Way, Parthenia Street and Reseda Boulevard, with cool islands tied to areas of higher vegetation cover. 3 “In the San Fernando Valley study area, the largest localized heat islands were associated with lowest vegetation canopy cover.” Taha and colleagues, California Energy Commission, 2018 [3] That is one modeled study from 2018, and the report notes that near downtown a different factor, lower albedo, drove the largest local heat islands. 3 So I do not read it as “trees fix everything.” I read it as a reason to check canopy on my own block first, because in this part of the city missing canopy is exactly where the heat concentrates. 03 Shade is not spread evenly If canopy matters that much, the next question is where it is. TreePeople’s analysis of Los Angeles tree canopy found that about a fifth (18%) of the city’s tree canopy grows where only 1% of the city’s population lives. That canopy sits in just five census block groups, which together hold under a tenth (8%) of the city’s land, in Pacific Palisades, Los Feliz, Brentwood and Shadow Hills. 4 The same analysis lists the areas in highest need of protective canopy: southeast county along the Interstate 110 corridor, the northeast part of the San Fernando Valley, and northern Los Angeles County. 4 My reading of that, and it is my reading, not theirs: shade is not missing evenly, it is missing in specific places, and the places are not hard to find. A study that starts from the city average will be wrong about its own block. A study that starts by counting the trees within sight of the site will not. 04 Air temperature is not what a body feels A weather station reports air temperature. A person standing on a sidewalk also takes in sun on their skin and heat given off by the paving and the walls around them. The combined effect is usually described with a measure called mean radiant temperature, which the coverage of the Pacoima cool pavement study calls “a measurement of thermal comfort.” 5 Fig. 2 A weather station reports air temperature. A person on a sidewalk also takes sun on the skin and heat from the surfaces around them. Concept sketch, not a measurement. This is why a 2-degree change in air temperature can be much less important than whether you are standing in shade. It is also why I try not to quote air temperature alone when I describe a site. The next note works through a real test of that idea in Pacoima. 05 A ten-minute check for any block You do not need a lab to apply this. Before I propose anything for a block, I do a short check, and every step is something a person can repeat from a phone and a sidewalk. Count the crowns. Stand at the middle of the block and count the trees whose canopy actually overhangs the walk, not the trees on the lot behind it. Write the number down, including zero. Note the face. Which way does the walk face? A west-facing walk takes the afternoon sun, a north-facing one mostly does not. Orientation decides which hour is the problem. Look at what is under the feet. Dark asphalt, light concrete, or planting. The Taha report links low albedo to heat islands near downtown, so surface color is a real variable. 3 Stand in it. Pick a sunny afternoon and stand in the sun for two minutes, then in the nearest shade for two. I have no instrument for this and I am not claiming a number. pages.x: A quarter mile is not the same walk in August | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Walking A quarter mile is not the same walk in August Transit planners measure how far people will walk. In a place that can hit 121 degrees, the better question is how much of that distance is in the sun. By Nathan Nov. 20, 2026 3 min read 4 sources Note 5 of 5 01 The rule of thumb Ask a transit planner how far people will walk to a bus stop and you get a familiar answer: about a quarter to a half mile, or five to fifteen minutes. 1 Agencies write the number into their guidelines. The Boston region’s metropolitan planning organization, for example, describes a coverage guideline that gives residents access within a one-quarter-mile walk of transit in areas with more than 5,000 people per square mile. 2 I should be honest about the weakness of my sourcing here. The five-to-fifteen-minute rule is repeated across planning documents, and I could not trace it back to one original study. It reads like folk knowledge that got written down. That does not make it wrong, but it does mean I should not lean on its exact figures. 02 What a quarter mile is The distance itself is simple. A mile is 5,280 feet, so a quarter mile is 1,320 feet. If I assume a walking pace of 3 miles per hour, which is a round number I am choosing and not a measured Valley pace, that is about 4.4 feet per second, and 1,320 feet takes 300 seconds: five minutes. Fig. 1 A quarter mile is 1,320 ft however it feels. What changes is how much of it is in the sun. The tree positions are illustrative, not a real street. Concept sketch. Five minutes is nothing on a mild day. The problem is that the planning rule describes the walk as if every five minutes costs the same, and in the Valley they do not. 03 Distance is not the whole cost Research on how far people actually walk to transit suggests the rule of thumb is not a hard limit anyway. One study of trip distance and walking to reach public transit concluded that the distance people are willing to walk appears to be much higher than the frequently cited rules of thumb of 0.25 to 0.5 miles. 3 I have read only the abstract, so I cannot say how well it applies to Los Angeles. The distance is the same. The walk is not. Nathan, this note That gap is why I do not think distance alone describes a walk. If willingness depends on the walk being tolerable, then shade, seating and surface can change who is willing to make it. I also know, from the first note in this series, that the Valley’s official record is 121°F. 4 On a day near that, five minutes at the same pace is not the same experience as five minutes in April. 04 A measure I want to try I want to add one number to my studies. I will call it the shaded share of a route. It is mine, and it is not an established standard, so read it as a proposal. The steps are simple enough that anyone could repeat them: Pick a route someone really takes, such as bus stop to storefront door. Walk it at a stated hour on a sunny day and mark each 100 feet as mostly shaded or mostly in sun. Report the shaded share as a fraction of the route, with the date, hour and orientation next to it. Draw the proposal and estimate the new share, labeled as an estimate. It is crude. Shade moves with the sun, and a pass at 3 p.m. says nothing about 11 a.m. But a crude, repeatable number beats a missing one, and it connects the distance people cite to the thing they feel. I have not collected any of this yet. Topanga Willows is the first place I would try it, because its walkway faces west. What I could not verify The origin of the five-to-fifteen-minute rule, and any Los Angeles-specific walking-distance data. The 3 mph pace is an assumption, so the five-minute figure is an estimate. I read only the abstract of the transit-walking study, and the Boston guideline is one region’s policy, not a national standard. The numbers are real. They also answer a smaller question than the one I care about. By Nathan Nov. 20, 2026 3 min read 2 sources Note 2 of 5 01 What was tested In the summer of 2022, more than 700,000 square feet of dark asphalt in Pacoima, a neighborhood in the northeast San Fernando Valley , was covered with a solar-reflective coating. The project was a partnership between the local nonprofit Climate Resolve and the roofing and waterproofing manufacturer GAF, which supplied the coating. 1 Haider Taha, an atmospheric modeler, studied it for a year, and the results were published in the journal Environmental Research Communications . 1 One thing to say plainly: GAF funded the study. The reporting says the company had no role in its design, data collection, modeling or analysis, and the paper was peer reviewed. 1 I think that is worth stating because the coating maker also benefits when the coating works. I have not read the paper itself, only coverage of it, so I cannot check the method myself. 02 What it found During an extreme heat event, the coated area had air temperatures as much as 3.5°F cooler than the adjacent neighborhood. On sunny days the reduction was up to 2.1°F, and on summer nights up to 0.5°F. The coating also lowered surface temperatures by up to around 10°F. 1 An earlier city report on a Los Angeles cool pavement installation found it averaged 12.8°F cooler than nearby uncoated black asphalt. 2 Fig. 1 Pacoima, where over 700,000 sq ft of dark asphalt was coated in summer 2022. Air and surface temperatures are different quantities on different scales, so read each panel on its own. Values are the maximum (“up to”) reductions the study reported, not averages, except the city figure. Sources 1 and 2 . Those are real cooling effects, and I do not want to wave them away. A surface that is 10°F cooler stores and re-radiates less heat after sunset, which is probably why the biggest air-temperature effect showed up during the extreme heat event rather than on ordinary days. That last part is my guess at the mechanism, not something the study claims in the coverage I read. 03 The catch is what you measure Almost every number above is about the air or the pavement. Neither is a person. The coverage notes that some researchers have found reflected sunlight can raise how hot pedestrians feel, and Taha said his study indicated an “improvement in thermal sensation.” He also said mean radiant temperature, a measure of thermal comfort, “goes up and down. It’s not always cooler,” and that “The overwhelming effect is the cooling.” 1 Both statements can be true. A reflective street can cool the neighborhood and still push some light onto the person walking on it. “No change in surface will protect the body from heat as effectively as preventing sunlight from hitting the body in the first place.” V. Kelly Turner, UCLA Luskin Center for Innovation, quoted by Smart Cities Dive [1] Turner, associate director of UCLA’s Luskin Center for Innovation, wrote in an email to the reporter that shade can cool people by up to 30°C, or 54°F, in hot, dry environments, and that reflective pavement does not have a large effect on air temperature unless it is deployed widely, and even then the benefit is moderate. 1 Note that her 54-degree figure is a different kind of number from the bars above: it describes how much cooler a person can be made, not how much cooler the street gets. I kept them out of the same chart for that reason. 04 Where paint still makes sense I do not read this as “never coat pavement.” Turner herself says reflective pavement is an appropriate choice where it is hard to replace heat-absorbing surfaces with something like vegetation, and where the goal is to reduce what the surface materials add to the area’s heat. She calls it one tool among many for the regional heat island , not a substitute for protecting people from the sun. 1 That fits how many lots are laid out. A parking aisle has to stay open for cars. A tree cannot go in the middle of it. A coating could, in principle, do some work there, and shade trees go on the edges, in planting strips and between rows. For my own studies I treat it this way, as a proposal and not a result: Shade first: trees, canopies and buildings between the sun and the people. Surface second: where trees physically cannot go, consider a reflective coat, and say what I do not know about its cost and upkeep. I have not priced it. Always say which quantity a claim is about: air, surface or body. What I could not verify I read the Smart Cities Dive coverage and the snippet of the city report, not the journal paper or the full report. The 12.8°F figure is from one city installation and compares to nearby black asphalt; it is not the same test as Pacoima. I do not have cost, durability or maintenance numbers for the coating, so I make no claim about value for money. Keep reading Two more notes from the same notebook The hottest day on record in L.A. pages.x: The sidewalk is a promise Los Angeles made in court | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Streets The sidewalk is a promise Los Angeles made in court A settlement, a $1.4 billion program and three small numbers explain why a sidewalk looks the way it does, and why it is harder to plant than it looks. By Nathan Nov. 20, 2026 4 min read 6 sources Note 4 of 5 01 How a settlement became a program Los Angeles runs a 30-year, $1.4 billion program to make its sidewalks accessible. The city launched it in December 2016. 1 The program exists because of a lawsuit, Willits v. City of Los Angeles , in which the plaintiffs alleged the city had failed to properly install and maintain accessible pedestrian facilities. 2 The city’s Bureau of Engineering says its Sidewalk Repair Program was initiated in response to the Willits settlement agreement. 3 One summary of the proposed agreement put the commitment at approximately $1.37 billion over 30 years. 4 The program is still being adjusted. The City Council approved a scoring system to prioritize repairs in January 2018, and in April 2026 approved a new Pedestrian Facility Severity Matrix. 1 Part of the program, the Access Request Program, makes repairs requested by or for people with a mobility disability who run into barriers such as broken sidewalks or missing or broken curb ramps. 1 The useful thing to take from this is that in Los Angeles a sidewalk is no longer leftover space beside the street. It is a legally tracked piece of infrastructure, and the reason is that people could not use it. 02 The three numbers that shape a sidewalk The federal Access Board’s guidelines for the public right-of-way set the technical rules for what counts as an accessible route. The board issued the final rule in August 2023. 5 I will say now that these are guidelines, and I have not checked which version Los Angeles’s own standards currently point to, so I use them here as the clearest published statement of the dimensions, not as the city’s legal requirement. These are the three that matter most for what I draw: Width. The continuous clear width of a pedestrian access route is 48 inches minimum, not counting the curb. Where it is narrower than 60 inches, passing spaces of 60 by 60 inches must be provided at intervals of 200 feet at most. 6 Slope across the walk. The cross slope of a pedestrian access route outside a crosswalk is 1:48, or 2.1%, at most. 6 Steps between slabs. Grade breaks must be flush. Changes in level of ¼ inch or less may be vertical. Between ¼ and ½ inch they must be beveled no steeper than 1:2, and above ½ inch up to 6 inches the slope can be 1:12 at most. 6 Fig. 1 The three numbers that shape most sidewalk design under the federal guidelines: clear width, cross slope, and the step between slabs. A tree trunk or pole inside the 48 in is a defect, not a feature. Concept sketch. “Changes in level of ¼ inch (6.4 mm) maximum shall be permitted to be vertical.” U.S. Access Board, Public Right-of-Way Accessibility Guidelines, R3 [6] 03 Why this matters for shade Put the two notes together and a tension appears. A tree needs lots of soil (see the previous note), and the sidewalk needs 48 clear inches with no vertical step bigger than a quarter inch. Roots lift slabs. Trunks grow into the clear width. Both are hard to design around when the strip is narrow, and it is why “just plant a tree” is never a complete drawing. I need to be careful not to overstate that. I know roots are a common reason for lifted slabs, but I have not found Los Angeles data on what share of the city’s sidewalk defects come from tree roots, so I cannot say how big the problem is here. I would not trust anyone who gave me a percentage without a source. What I take from it as a design rule is concrete. For each tree I propose, my drawing should show the clear width left beside it, the soil it will reach, and what happens at the slab joint if a root lifts it. If I cannot draw those three things, I should say so and not label the tree as solved. 04 What I check before I draw a bench or a tree A sidewalk plan is mostly a list of things that cannot be in the way. Here is the short version of how I now read a site, using the dimensions above. Measure the clear width at the narrowest point, which is usually a pole, a hydrant, a signal box or a tree guard, not the middle of the slab. Look along the joints for steps. A step taller than the quarter inch the guidelines allow to stay vertical is a defect to note, and one beyond half an inch needs a ramped transition. 6 Check whether the walk is public. On Topanga Canyon Boulevard in my first study, the planting strip is public right-of-way, so anything there is a request to the agencies, not something an owner can just build. Add a bench or tree only where the 48 inches survive. If they do not, the furniture goes on private land behind the walk. 05 What I do not know What I could not verify I read the program’s own pages and the Access Board’s text, not the settlement agreement. I have not found how many miles of sidewalk have been repaired so far, or whether the program is on schedule. I have not checked which accessibility standard the city currently enforces; the numbers above are the federal guideline text. That list is also my to-do list for a longer note. A real answer to “is the program working?” needs the city’s progress reports, and I have not read them. pages.x: A shade tree is a soil problem first | Notes | Redrawn Valley ← Notes Trees and soil A shade tree is a soil problem first Everyone agrees the Valley needs more trees. Almost nobody draws the hole they have to grow in. The arithmetic is simple, and it changes what a street can hold. By Nathan Nov. 20, 2026 4 min read 4 sources Note 3 of 5 01 The rule of thumb everyone repeats If you ask how much soil a big street tree needs, you hear a number: about 1,000 cubic feet. It is a long-repeated rule of thumb. DeepRoot, a company that sells soil-cell systems for street trees, calls it “a helpful rudimentary rule of thumb” and says the industry has moved beyond it. 1 A seller of tree-soil products has a reason to say more is better, so I treat that as a source for the existence of the rule and not as proof of the right number. A neutral reference is the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency’s stormwater manual, which lists example minimum tree soil volumes from different jurisdictions. Among them: 30 cubic meters (1,059 cubic feet) of soil per tree, and 20 cubic meters (706 cubic feet) per tree when the volume is shared between trees. 2 I do not know which jurisdictions those two entries belong to, only that they are listed as real requirements. 02 A second way to get the same number The American Society of Landscape Architects offers a different route: trees need about 1.5 to 2 cubic feet of loam soil per square foot of the area under their mature canopy . 3 That makes the volume depend on how big the tree gets, which is more honest than one number for every species. Try it with a tree that has a 30-foot crown. I picked 30 feet as an example, it is not a measured tree. A circle 30 feet across has an area of about 707 square feet (π × 15²). At 1.5 to 2 cubic feet per square foot, that is roughly 1,060 to 1,410 cubic feet of soil. That lands right around the 1,000-to-1,059 figures above, which is the reason I trust the order of magnitude even though I do not trust any single rule to the last foot. A tree is a bet on how much soil it can reach. Nathan, this note The academic version of the idea goes back at least to 1991, when Lindsey and Bassuk published a method for specifying soil volumes to meet the water needs of mature street trees and trees in containers. 4 I have read its title and abstract page, not the full paper, so I am citing it for the existence of the approach, not for its numbers. 03 The tree well next to it Now compare that with the hole most sidewalk trees are given. I do not have a measured sample, so I use an assumption and label it: a small tree well of 4 by 4 feet, dug 3 feet deep. That is 48 cubic feet. Against a 1,000-cubic-foot target it is about one twenty-first, and against the 1,059 figure about one twenty-second. Those ratios are my arithmetic on my assumed well. Fig. 1 Plan view at one scale: the soil a mature shade tree is commonly said to need, set against a small tree well. The 1,000 cu ft figure is a rule of thumb, and 48 cu ft is my assumed size for a small well. Arithmetic: 1,000 ÷ 3 ft = 333 sq ft, about 18 × 18 ft. Concept sketch. Spread over 3 feet of depth, 1,000 cubic feet needs about 333 square feet of soil surface, which is roughly 18 feet by 18 feet. The picture matters more than the ratio. A sidewalk planting strip is often only a few feet wide, so the soil a tree needs does not fit under the strip. It has to run under the paving, the parking lot or the road edge, where it competes with everything else buried there. 04 How I would check a real strip If I were sizing soil for a real planting strip, I would work in this order, and I would stop at the first step I could not complete. Measure the strip. Width, length and the clear width left on the walk beside it. The surface area available is the first limit. Find what is below. Request utility information and look for as-built drawings before assuming any depth is free. Pick a tree and its mature crown. Then apply the 1.5 to 2 cubic feet per square foot rule from the landscape architects as a first pass. 3 Compare with what fits. Multiply the strip’s area by a usable depth. If the answer is far under the target, the choices are a smaller tree, shared soil with a neighbor, or a different location, not a hopeful drawing of a large tree. The honest result is often “a smaller tree than I wanted.” That is still better shade than a large tree that dies young in a small hole. 05 What that does to a plan This is the part I find most interesting as someone heading toward civil engineering. The tree is the easy line on the drawing. The hard parts are underneath: Utilities. Water, sewer, gas and electric lines already occupy the ground. Before drawing any soil volume I would need a locate and as-built drawings, not an assumption that the ground is empty. Sharing. The 706-cubic-foot shared figure suggests one way out: a continuous soil trench under a row of trees, instead of separate pits. That is my reading of the shared-volume entry, and I have not seen it detailed for Los Angeles. Paving on top. If the soil is under a walk or lot, the paving has to carry loads over it, which is a structural design question, and the reason systems like soil cells exist. I have not engineered that and am not claiming a solution. Width on the surface. The tree and its tree guard cannot narrow the walkway below the accessible minimum. The next note covers that rule. Topanga Willows, my first study, is where I ran into this: a long west-facing storefront, one small tree, and a planting strip that belongs to the public right-of-way. so it is the first place to check whether this arithmetic holds up on a real site. Read the study → What I could not verify The 4 × 4 × 3 ft well is my assumption of a small well, not a surveyed one. I do not know the soil-volume requirement in the City of Los Angeles code, and I do not claim one here. The rule-of-thumb figures vary by source and by species; none of these is a design value for a specific tree. K

Part 1 of 4 The site What is there, and why it is hot 01 The site A building on the sidewalk, a parking lot behind it Topanga Willows fills the east side of Topanga Canyon Boulevard for one block, from Providencia Street down to Dumetz Road. The building is one long single-story bar, roughly 210 feet by 50, set right on the sidewalk with red awnings on both faces. [31] The owner lists it at 9,809 square feet. [1] The map shows a nail salon, a cleaner, a quilt shop, The Yoga Center and a pizza place; the owner also lists Starbucks and Yogis Grill. [1] [31] All the parking is behind the building, on the east: four rows of angled stalls on two one-way aisles, about 68 stalls, with driveways on Providencia and on Dumetz. Houses back onto the east edge. The whole lot has one small tree in it. [31] The owner counts about 30,463 vehicles a day on Topanga Canyon and 11,457 on Dumetz, with 114,413 people living within three miles. [1] A second listing gives 36,641 and 9,424, so I treat both as rough. [2] The orientation is the whole story. Because the building sits on the west side of its lot, it shades only the first row of stalls late in the day. The rest of the lot is in the sun from morning on. And the side people actually walk along, the storefronts on Topanga Canyon, faces west into the afternoon sun. One constraint: Topanga Canyon Boulevard is State Route 27, a Caltrans road. [29] The planted strip between the curb and the sidewalk is public right-of-way, so anything there is a request to the agencies, not something the owner can just build. Fig. 2: Existing conditions.
